author: Declaration Desk
title: Liberty cases to reach a bench within two working days, CJI says on Constitution Day
dek: Chief Justice Surya Kant set out the Supreme Court's listing rules and priority for elderly, disabled and poor litigants, saying it must not remain a court of the privileged.
body:
Cases involving personal liberty or urgent interim relief must now reach a Supreme Court bench within two working days, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said on Thursday, as he set out how the court has changed the way it decides which cases are heard and when. Speaking at the court's Constitution Day function, attended by President Droupadi Murmu, he said the Supreme Court must not remain a court where access depends on who is asking.

He acknowledged that the institution had at times been seen as a court of the privileged, where an out-of-turn hearing could seem to depend on who sought it rather than how urgent the matter was, and where wealthier litigants could reach it at the earliest stage of a dispute. "We are on a continuous mission to ensure that no citizen ever finds the doors of justice closed," he said, according to reports of the speech.

## What the court has changed

The Chief Justice listed the reforms in place:

- Automatic listing: fresh cases are listed without lawyers having to ask for a date in open court, a practice known as "mentioning" that favoured those with senior counsel on hand.
- The two-working-day rule for matters involving personal liberty or urgent interim relief.
- Priority for litigants who face greater barriers: persons with disabilities, acid-attack survivors, citizens over 80, people below the poverty line and those represented through legal aid. "The least we can do is to ensure that their turn comes in good time," he said.
- Criteria announced in advance and applied uniformly, so that no one receives undue favour, he said.

He also pointed to technology: video hearings that let lawyers argue from places such as Kohima and Kochi; livestreamed Constitution Bench hearings transcribed with AI; SUVAS, the court's AI-assisted software that translates judgments into Indian languages; a "One Case, One Data" system tracing a case from the taluka court to the Supreme Court; and an AI assistant to guide litigants through procedure. A judgment citizens cannot read cannot truly belong to them, he said.

The court did not publish figures on how many cases have been listed under the new rules, and the Chief Justice gave none.

## Criticism of the judiciary

At a separate function organised by the Supreme Court Bar Association the same day, the Chief Justice said a confident institution "must have the capacity to engage with citizens" when it is criticised, but that criticism "must not be motivated with political agendas or personal gains to attack the institution". "Institutional restraint, mutual respect and accountability are, therefore, essential," he said, according to reports.

## Background

Constitution Day, 26 November, marks the adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly in 1949. Delays in listing have long been one of the main complaints about the Supreme Court, where tens of thousands of cases are pending and where getting a matter heard quickly has often depended on mentioning it before the Chief Justice. Justice Surya Kant took office as Chief Justice in November 2025.

Also present were Justice Vikram Nath, Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal and Attorney General R. Venkataramani.

## What happens next

The listing rules apply now. Whether the two-day promise holds will show in the court's own data on pending and urgent matters, which it publishes through the National Judicial Data Grid.
